question: A previously healthy 16-year-old boy comes to the physician because of a pruritic rash on the chest that has become progressively larger over the past 10 days. It is not painful. He is sexually active with two female partners and uses condoms inconsistently. He works part-time as a lifeguard. He has no family history of serious illness. He does not smoke. He drinks 5–6 beers on weekends. His temperature is 36.7°C (98°F), pulse is 66/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. A photograph of the rash is shown below. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "16-year-old boy with pruritic rash" -> "rash progressively larger over 10 days" -> "possible dermatological condition" -> "consider common skin conditions" -> "evaluate for tinea corporis" -> "topical miconazole indicated for fungal infection" -> 85%

CHAIN: "16-year-old boy with pruritic rash" -> "rash not painful" -> "less likely to be infectious or inflammatory" -> "consider non-infectious causes" -> "evaluate for eczema or contact dermatitis" -> "topical hydrocortisone may provide relief" -> 75%

CHAIN: "16-year-old boy with pruritic rash" -> "rash on chest" -> "consider environmental exposure" -> "lifeguard role suggests sun exposure" -> "possible sunburn or photodermatitis" -> "phototherapy may be appropriate" -> 70%

CHAIN: "16-year-old boy with pruritic rash" -> "rash progressively larger" -> "indicates potential worsening condition" -> "reassurance may not be sufficient" -> "topical treatment likely needed" -> "topical erythromycin not indicated for this presentation" -> 60%
analysis: The patient's presentation of a pruritic rash that has progressively enlarged over 10 days, along with his history of being sexually active and working as a lifeguard, raises suspicion for a dermatological condition such as tinea corporis (ringworm) or another fungal infection. Given the options, topical miconazole (an antifungal) would be appropriate if a fungal infection is suspected. However, if the rash is more consistent with a non-infectious dermatitis, topical hydrocortisone could be considered. Without the photograph, it's difficult to definitively diagnose, but the most common and likely cause in a young male with a pruritic rash is a fungal infection, making topical miconazole the most appropriate next step in management.
